feedback: If a learner is surprised how far they must walk to the outer planets, confirm this is the point: standard diagrams compress these distances and seed the misconception of even spacing.
At this distance scale, correctly scaled planets would be very small. They can share one honest scale, but may be hard to see; label enlarged planet symbols clearly if using them.
activities.intendedInsight: The true separations in the solar system are vast and grow enormously outward; a readable page-sized diagram with visible planets usually distorts this, which is why mental models are often wrong.
learnerActions: Build a scaled-distance model: using a chosen scale, place the Sun at one end of a field or corridor and pace out or measure where each planet falls
Notice physically that the inner planets are bunched close together while the outer planets are strikingly far away

Compare distances proportionally, for example Neptune is about thirty times Earth’s average distance from the Sun. An optional flythrough can display a light-travel-time counter; label any time compression rather than implying light crosses the system instantly.

Discuss why a page-sized model cannot readily show recognisable planet discs and their distances at one readable scale. A true shared-scale model is possible, but the planets become tiny at a scale that fits the whole system.
activities.title: Pace out the real distances

feedback: If a learner says every planet takes 'about a year,' compare Mercury (88 days) with Neptune (~165 years) to break the assumption.
If a learner guesses outer planets are 'shorter, they move faster,' point out the data shows the opposite: both the larger orbit and the slower orbital speed lengthen the year.
If a learner knows outer planets take longer but can't say why, prompt them toward 'bigger orbit + slower motion = longer year.'
activities.intendedInsight: Learners discover for themselves the ordered relationship — farther = longer year — and can justify it, instead of reciting it.
learnerActions: Work from a real data table of planet distance from the Sun and orbital period
Plot or line up distance against period and describe the pattern you find
Compare specific cases: Mercury takes about 88 days for one orbit while Neptune takes about 165 Earth years
Explain in your own words why outer planets have longer years (bigger path travelled more slowly) rather than just stating the fact
activities.title: Plot distance against orbital period

feedback: If a learner lists Pluto among the planets, explain it hasn't cleared its orbital neighbourhood, which is what distinguishes a dwarf planet from a planet.

If a learner uses 'asteroid' and 'comet' interchangeably, contrast them: asteroid = rock/metal, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter; comet = ice and dust on a long looping orbit that grows a tail near the Sun.
An ion tail is approximately antisolar; a dust tail can curve. Use the illustrated tail type and do not infer the comet’s travel direction merely from a tail as if it were a smoke trail.
If a learner pictures the asteroid belt as a dense, dangerous field of tightly packed rocks, clarify that it is mostly empty space with vast gaps between the bodies.
activities.intendedInsight: The four body types are defined by criteria (orbit-clearing, roundness, composition, orbit shape), so categorisation is reasoning, not recall; dwarf planets are a distinct category, not just 'small planets.'
learnerActions: Sort mystery objects into planet / dwarf planet / asteroid / comet using criteria, not memory

For each, apply the defining tests: Does it orbit the Sun and is it round? Has it cleared its orbital neighbourhood? Is it a small rocky/metal body (mostly in the belt)? Is it icy on a long elliptical orbit that grows a tail near the Sun?
Explain why Pluto is a dwarf planet: round and orbiting the Sun, but it shares its orbital zone (hasn't cleared it) — the same class as Ceres and Eris

Compare a comet’s ion tail, which points approximately away from the Sun under the solar wind, with its often curved dust tail shaped by radiation pressure and the comet’s orbital motion. Neither should simply be treated as a trail left behind the comet.
activities.title: Sort bodies by their defining criteria

feedback: If all round objects are called planets, compare Earth and its Moon and identify the satellite relationship.
Do not imply that every planet has moons, or give an undated total for rapidly updated moon counts.
activities.intendedInsight: Moons are natural satellites within the wider solar system; roundness and a location near the Sun are not sufficient to classify a body as a planet.
learnerActions: Use inset diagrams to identify Earth’s Moon and Mars’s moons Phobos and Deimos as natural satellites.
Distinguish a planet or dwarf planet from a natural satellite bound to and orbiting another body; show that dwarf planets can have moons too.
Explain why being round is not enough to make Earth’s Moon a planet, and compare a satellite view with the wider Sun-centred system.
activities.title: Locate moons as natural satellites
